extracted.intended_audience: university mathematics instructors, mathematics education researchers, and curriculum designers
extracted.subtask_description: Translating informal theorems/definitions (especially from calculus) into equivalent formal predicate-calculus statements and using those formalizations to build/validate proof frameworks; includes pedagogical implications for teaching undergraduates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpack informal statements into formal predicate-calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate an informally written mathematical statement into an equivalent formal version using quantifiers, variables, connectives, and (where appropriate) universes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper gives sample correct unpackings for each informal statement and treats all logically equivalent formal forms as equally correct. Very simple syntax errors (e.g., a missing right parenthesis) are ignored when judging correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify every actual variable and specify its universe
rubrics_metrics.description: All free/actual variables in the unpacked/formal statement must be explicitly quantified and have their domains (universes) specified when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later task instructions asked students to 'make sure all variables were quantified and had universes.' Failure to quantify actual variables was counted as an error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the correct type and order of quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Place universal and existential quantifiers in the correct positions and order; interchanging them or using the wrong type changes meaning and is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an innocent-looking interchange of universal and existential quantifiers radically altered the meaning of a statement (illustrated in Statement 1). Using an existential where a universal is required (or vice versa) was a common student error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not quantify a variable twice or quantify bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid redundant quantification (quantifying the same variable twice) and avoid attempting to quantify variables that are already bound within the scope of the expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors counted quantifying a variable twice and quantifying bound variables as student errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map colloquial words to the correct logical connective
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace English connective words (e.g., 'means', 'if', 'whenever') with the logically correct connective(s) when formalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, in Statement 4 the word 'means' must be replaced by the appropriate logical connective(s). Failing to do so (or replacing with the wrong connective) was treated as an error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse 'if' with 'if-and-only-if' (iff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the distinction between implication ('if') and bi-conditional ('if-and-only-if'); confusing them is treated as a substantive error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although in some contexts this might be a minor oversight, the study counted confusing 'if' with 'iff' as an error when it would significantly alter what one would expect to see in a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all hypotheses and conclusions; omissions count as errors
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct unpacking must preserve the full content of the original informal statement; omitting part of a hypothesis or a conclusion is an error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigators counted as errors anything that would significantly alter what one would expect to see in a proof, including omitted hypotheses or conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve ambiguities using domain knowledge when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous informal statements should be disambiguated by appeal to relevant domain knowledge to determine the intended unpacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that some ambiguities can be resolved because an expert's domain knowledge shows one unpacking to be clearly false; they give examples involving compact semigroups where expert knowledge resolves potential ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat logically equivalent formalizations as equally correct for scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing student unpackings, accept any formalization that is logically equivalent to the intended formal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring ignored equivalent alternative formal forms; very small syntax errors were also ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary universal quantification and redundant quotation of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing proofs/formalizations, do not include unnecessary universal quantifiers (e.g., arguing about all epsilons simultaneously) and avoid over-quoting definitions/theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper observes that undergraduates commonly unnecessarily include universal quantifiers and quote definitions excessively; mathematical style typically avoids these to reduce cognitive load during validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent symbol meaning and avoid redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not vary the meaning of symbols within an argument and avoid redundant statements that obscure logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistent symbol usage and redundancy may not be errors in everyday arguments but are usually avoided in proofs; such issues impede validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure proof framework matches the unpacked statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's embedded proof-framework should correspond appropriately to the logical form of the theorem; validators check that the starting assumptions (e.g., 'let a,f,g be arbitrary') align with the theorem's unpacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example validation shows the validator checking that the proof begins with arbitrary objects matching the universal structure of the theorem; line 1 in the sample proof serves this role even if experts sometimes omit it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation may require reconstructing omitted steps and domain knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Validators should be prepared to expand the written proof by inserting omitted justifications, domain-knowledge steps, or intermediate lines necessary to verify correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that writers produce proofs for an idealized reader; actual validators may need to create additions, so validation can be creative and lengthy. Example: justifying the triangle inequality step or filling in algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make multiple passes through a proof when validating
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid working-memory overload and missed dependencies, validators should read proofs multiple times, checking and re-checking earlier and later steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns that inserting justifications late in checking can overload working memory and suggests multiple passes as a guard against missing parts of the validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present theorems both informally and formally for teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: In instruction, present theorems and definitions in both an intuitive informal form and an explicit formalized form to support both understanding and careful validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a teaching recommendation: presenting both forms accommodates intuition and facilitates learning to validate proofs; translating definitions into symbolic form helped students see logical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide explicit instruction and practice on validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach students explicit strategies for validation (not just proof writing), including asking why an argument proves the stated theorem and explaining why proposed solutions should be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend explicit instruction on validation (not restricted to proofs) and suggest exercises like explaining why an argument proves a specific theorem as part of course practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish proofs from explanatory or supplementary remarks in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting material, clearly separate the proof from explanatory remarks, illustrations, cautionary notes, and comments on proof structure (treat these as annotations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making this distinction explicit gives students prototypical examples of proofs and helps them learn to validate proofs; authors suggest treating nonessential remarks as annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build statement images via examples, visualization, and student-produced arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use prototypical examples, visualizations, and student-generated argumentation to create strong mental statement-images that support later unpacking and proof-framework construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper gives an example (complex unit disk) showing how an illustrative example becomes a prototypical image, and recommends encouraging student reflection and argumentation early in schooling to build an experiential base for proof.
